title: Detect and mitigate quota-evasion via request-slicing and tiny-fragment bursts
creator: Ava Chen
description:
Problem statement:
Customers and internal audits have identified a pattern where clients slice large payloads into many tiny requests (1-5 tokens) or issue micro-bursts after hitting per-request or per-minute quota thresholds. This behavior allows them to effectively skirt per-request minimums and some coarse quota enforcement, leading to both revenue leakage and unfair resource consumption. The slice/burst pattern also complicates streaming accounting because many fragments produce many short-lived KV cache states and billable fragments.

Observed examples:
- A single tenant sends 600 requests in 60s, each request returns 2 tokens; previous per-request minimums and naive per-call billing resulted in undercounting of what should be treated as a single logical request.
- Proxy clients open many parallel short streams to distribute load and avoid short-window rate-limits.
- Clients intentionally emit tiny edits repeatedly to evade quota throttles on long prompt replay detection.

Goals:
1) Detect request-slicing and micro-burst patterns reliably across tenants.
2) Apply deterministic normalization for billing so that logically aggregated work is billed fairly.
3) Mitigate at enforcement layer (soft-block, slow-down, provisional credits) while avoiding false positives for legitimate bursty workloads (e.g., interactive editors).

Proposed design overview:
- Ingest-time aggregation: add a short-lived (configurable, default 5s) aggregation window keyed by tenant+route+api_key_fingerprint. Within that window, collapse small requests whose combined token footprint exceeds a configurable threshold into a single billing unit for the purpose of quota calculation. The aggregation is ephemeral for enforcement and billing normalization but does not modify payloads to backflow to customers.
- Heuristics & risk scoring: maintain sliding-window features per tenant (requests/sec, median tokens/request, 95p tokens/request, parallel stream count, variance) and compute a quota-evasion risk score using a lightweight logistic model. Use thresholds to trigger mitigations and investigations.
- Enforcement options (tiered):
  * Observability-only: flag and surface alerts to Console when score > medium.
  * Soft mitigation: temporarily increase per-request token floor for the tenant (provisional) and/or slow acceptance (linear backoff) for new fragments for up to N seconds.
  * Hard mitigation: apply rate-limit or require tenant to route through dedicated capacity (escalation).
- Billing normalization: when aggregation kicks in, generate a normalized billing record that sums token usage across the window and attributes it to the tenant with a special tag \"normalized_from_slices\". This enables audits and retroactive charge adjustments when necessary.
- Telemetry & auditing: emit event stream entries for each aggregation occurrence with sample payload hashes, candidate grouping keys, and chosen mitigation. Link to a shadow simulation pipeline for historical replay and false-positive tuning.

Operational constraints and trade-offs:
- Latency impact: the aggregation window is short (<= 5s) and only used for billing/quotas; streaming API remains low-latency for output. We must ensure p99 progress latency increases by <5%. Avoid blocking critical synchronous paths.
- Memory/scale: ephemeral windows per-tenant will increase memory usage; implement eviction and an LRU cap. Use approximate counters (bounded) to lower cost.
- Legal/billing: normalization changes must be transparent and reversible; create audit trails and opt-in pilot for a subset of tenants before full rollout.

Acceptance criteria (see separate field for checklist):

Implementation notes and tasks:
- Backend: add aggregation window microservice (or extend existing metering worker) to maintain per-tenant short windows and emit normalized billing records.
- Runtime: integrate into rate-limiter decision path and token-accounting finalizer. Ensure idempotency keys for normalized records.
- Console: dashboard surface for flagged tenants and a % of normalized billing adjustments in the last 30 days.
- Tests: unit tests for grouping heuristics, load tests simulating 10k tenants with bursty patterns, e2e billing accuracy tests vs. golden ledger.
- Docs & customer comms: PRD + runbook + support FAQ for affected customers explaining provisional credits and appeal process.

Links:
- Design doc (confluence): https://redwood.atlassian.net/l/c/MM-example-aggregate-metering
- Simulation notebook (drive): https://drive.redwood.ai/simulations/quota_evasion_v2.ipynb
acceptance_criteria: Normalized billing records created for aggregated windows and visible in audit logs
False positive rate < 1% on historical replay dataset used in simulation
p99 tail latency increase < 5% when aggregation enabled on a 20% canary
E2E billing reconciliation test passes against golden ledger for 1000 synthetic tenants
Console shows a breakdown of normalization events and mitigation actions
rollout_plan: 1) Canary (5% tenants, telemetry-only) for 2 weeks to gather false-positive stats; 2) Canary (20% tenants) with soft mitigations and billing normalization enabled for 1 week; 3) Ramp to 50% pending audit sign-off; 4) Full rollout after legal approval. Include opt-out flag for enterprise tenants during pilot.
tests: load: 10k tenant bursts at peak QPS
notes: We should avoid automatic refunds without manual review; provisional credits should be used so that billing adjustments are reversible. Coordinate with finance for an appeals workflow.
